To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) human ex-vivo expanded erythroblats (EBs) can lodge in the spleens of recipient mice, where they are destroyed; 2) the presence of human EB-derived cells in the blood of the recipient mice can be detected by bioluminescence; and 3) human EBs injected in splenectomised mice can lodge in the liver and bone marrow, and persist for at least 4 days.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the biology of the erythroblastic cell and its potential use in the treatment of anemia.
the development of a new generation of blood products, based on the expansion of erythrocyte progenitors ex vivo.
the development of new therapeutic approaches for the management of anemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data is very interesting and the model is a very useful tool to investigate the potential therapeutic value of ex vivo generated EBs.
the ex-vivo expanded erythroblast population is able to engraft and persist in the mouse model.
the study is well designed, the results are interesting and informative, and the conclusions are appropriate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an in vivo model for the tracking of human erythroblasts expanded ex vivo from different sources.
the ex vivo expanded erythroblast (EBs) can be tracked and quantified in NOD/SCIDs.
we have established a mouse model that will be very valuable for investigating the in vivo function of expanded ex vivo human EBs derived under different culture conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spleen is the main barrier to the survival of human erythroblasts in mice.
the presence of spleen in the recipient mice represents a barrier to the engraftment and persistence of ex-vivo expanded human erythroblasts.
human erythropoiesis in the spleen is a major barrier to the development of human erythroblast-based therapeutics.
